title: Sony Music, Warner sue Anthropic, alleging a "brazen campaign" of intellectual
content:
Sony Music Publishing, Warner Chappell and numerous other music publishers have sued Anthropic and co-founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann, alleging the AI lab conducted a “brazen campaign of illegally torrenting, scraping, and downloading copyrighted works.”
The lawsuit, which was filed late Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, was first reported by Music Business Worldwide. The publishers accuse Anthropic of “blatant theft” by using thousands of copyrighted works to train its AI model Claude.
“We disagree with the publishers’ claims and we intend to defend ourselves robustly in court,” an Anthropic spokesperson wrote in an emailed statement sent to TechCrunch.
This isn’t the first intellectual property lawsuit Anthropic has faced. Some of the same lawyers behind this lawsuit also represent Concord Music Group and Universal Music Group in a case filed in January and led the Bartz v. Anthropic case, in which a group of authors accused Anthropic of using copyrighted works to train products like Claude. Anthropic was ordered to pay $1.5 billion in the landmark Bartz case after a judge ruled that while it was legal for the AI lab to use copyrighted works, it was not legal to acquire that content through piracy.
While the cases make similar arguments, there are key differences. This latest lawsuit is particularly broad and builds off the other cases, including by accusing Anthropic of “flagrant piracy” through illegal torrenting to obtain millions of copies of books, including those that contain lyrics and sheet music.
Article was updated to include Anthropic’s comment.

report.summary: Sony Music and Warner Chappell sue Anthropic for alleged copyright theft via torrenting and scraping to train Claude.
report.background: Anthropic faces a new wave of legal pressure from the music industry. The lawsuit, filed in Northern California, accuses Anthropic of illegally obtaining copyrighted sheet music, lyrics, and books through torrenting and scraping to train its Claude models. This follows the Bartz v. Anthropic ruling, which allowed using copyrighted works for AI training but prohibited piracy to obtain them—Anthropic was ordered to pay $1.5 billion. The new suit, brought by major publishers including Sony Music Publishing and Warner Chappell, is broader, citing 'flagrant piracy' and building on prior cases from Concord Music Group and Universal Music Group. Anthropic denies the claims and vows to defend itself. The case highlights the unresolved tension between AI training needs and intellectual property rights, especially as courts begin distinguishing between lawful access and unlawful acquisition methods.
key_points: Major music publishers sued Anthropic for allegedly using torrenting and scraping to obtain copyrighted works for AI training. The lawsuit names co-founders Dario Amodei and Benjamin Mann and explicitly accuses the lab of a 'brazen campaign' of intellectual property theft.

This case builds on prior litigation, including the $1.5 billion Bartz ruling. In Bartz, the judge said using copyrighted content for AI training was legal, but acquiring it through piracy was not—a distinction that shapes the new publishers' claims.

The scope is unusually broad. It covers millions of books, lyrics, and sheet music, and alleges 'flagrant piracy' rather than just unauthorized training. The publishers argue Anthropic knew the works were copyrighted yet still downloaded them illegally.

Anthropic's defense maintains that the claims are baseless. A spokesperson said the company disagrees and intends to 'defend ourselves robustly in court,' suggesting a prolonged legal battle that could set precedent for AI data sourcing practices.

Legal outcomes may hinge on how Anthropic obtained training data. If the court finds evidence of torrenting copyrighted works, that could violate prior court precedent—even if the ultimate use in AI training is deemed transformative or lawful.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this case sharpens the boundary between permissible training on copyrighted material and illegal acquisition. If publishers win, AI labs may need to overhaul data collection practices, avoiding torrents and even automated scraping of protected works. Developers will face higher costs for licensed datasets and stricter internal compliance checks. For users, the outcome could affect AI features that generate song lyrics or analyze music, potentially limiting functionality until licensing agreements are in place. More broadly, the suit signals that courts are scrutinizing not just outputs but the methods used to obtain training data—a shift that could influence how future AI models are built and governed.
report.tools: For those following AI copyright issues, watch tools like the Open Source Licensing Checklist (OSLC) for data provenance, and Fairlearn for auditing model compliance. Also monitor the Python-based 'trafilatura' for responsible web scraping, and the 'Content Authenticity Initiative' ecosystem for content provenance. Legal databases like CourtListener can track Anthropic's cases.
